title: Shilajit and Ashwagandha Together: Benefits & Dosage
description: Should you take Shilajit and Ashwagandha together? What the human research actually shows, sensible dosages, timing, and who should be cautious. From Salxir.
bodyHtml:
Two of the most talked-about botanicals in Ayurveda have very different day jobs. Shilajit is a mineral-rich resin that seeps from Himalayan rock in the summer heat. Ashwagandha is a root that has been used for centuries to help the body cope with stress. Taking Shilajit and Ashwagandha together has become one of the most popular adaptogen stacks going — and unlike a lot of supplement pairings, there is a reasonable logic behind it. Here is what each one actually does, what the human research supports, and how to combine them sensibly. If the resin itself is new to you, start with our pillar guide on what Shilajit is and where it comes from.

Why taking Shilajit and Ashwagandha together makes sense

The case for stacking rests on one idea: they barely overlap. Ashwagandha's best-studied effects run through the stress axis — the hormonal loop that governs cortisol. Shilajit's work sits closer to nutrition and cellular energy: trace minerals, fulvic acid, and the machinery your cells use to make ATP. One helps dial down the noise; the other helps supply the raw materials. In practice, people describe the combination as steadier rather than stimulating.

An honest caveat before we go further: almost every good clinical trial has tested these two separately. There is no large randomised trial of the combination itself. What we have is solid evidence for each ingredient on its own, plus a plausible, non-overlapping mechanism. That is a decent reason to try a stack — not proof that one plus one equals three.

What Ashwagandha brings: stress, sleep and strength

Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) has the stronger stress-related evidence base of the pair.

  • Cortisol and perceived stress. In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 64 chronically stressed adults, 600 mg a day of a standardised root extract for 60 days was associated with a roughly 28% drop in serum cortisol versus placebo, alongside better scores on standard stress questionnaires.
  • Strength and body composition. A 2015 trial published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition followed men through eight weeks of resistance training. The 600 mg group gained more muscle size and strength than placebo, with a modest rise in testosterone.
  • Sleep. Pooled analyses of small trials suggest a modest improvement in sleep quality, most consistent in people who already sleep badly, at doses of 600 mg or more taken for at least eight weeks.

Across the literature, the effective range is roughly 250–600 mg per day of a standardised root extract. More is not obviously better.

What Shilajit brings: minerals, fulvic acid and cellular energy

Shilajit is not a single compound. Purified resin contains fulvic acid, dibenzo-alpha-pyrones, and a broad spread of trace minerals — which is why its effects tend to be described as foundational rather than dramatic.

  • Hormonal markers in older men. A 90-day placebo-controlled study in Andrologia gave 250 mg of purified Shilajit twice daily to healthy men aged 45–55 and reported significant increases in total testosterone, DHEA-S and FSH compared with placebo.
  • Muscle fatigue. An eight-week trial of 500 mg a day in healthy adults found better retention of muscle strength after a fatiguing exercise protocol than placebo.
  • Mitochondrial support. Laboratory work suggests fulvic-acid constituents help stabilise coenzyme Q10 and support ATP production. This is genuinely interesting, but it is still largely preclinical — worth knowing, not worth over-promising.

Shilajit and Ashwagandha dosage: how much, and when

A sensible starting point for most adults:

  • Shilajit: a pea-sized amount of resin, roughly 300–500 mg, once a day dissolved in warm water, tea or milk. Capsules and tablets land in a similar range per serving.
  • Ashwagandha: 300–600 mg of a standardised root extract, taken with food to reduce the chance of mild stomach upset.

On timing, many people take Shilajit in the morning and Ashwagandha in the evening, on the reasoning that one supports daytime energy and the other supports winding down. That split is convention rather than settled science, and taking both at the same time is fine if it makes the habit stick. We go deeper on this in our guide to the best time to take Shilajit.

One practical tip that costs nothing: introduce them one at a time. Run Shilajit alone for two weeks, then add Ashwagandha. If something helps — or disagrees with you — you will actually know which one did it. And give the stack eight to twelve weeks before judging it. Both ingredients build slowly; neither works like caffeine.

Who should be cautious

This stack is not for everyone, and we would rather say so plainly.

  • Ashwagandha has rare but documented case reports of idiosyncratic liver injury. It may also raise thyroid hormone levels, so it warrants medical advice if you have a thyroid condition or take thyroid medication. People with autoimmune conditions, those on sedatives, and anyone pregnant or breastfeeding should speak to a clinician first.
  • Shilajit is only as clean as its processing. Raw, unpurified resin scraped straight from rock can carry heavy metals, which is exactly why third-party lab testing is non-negotiable. It also contains iron, so it is worth checking with a doctor if you have an iron-overload condition such as haemochromatosis.

If you take prescription medication of any kind, run both past your doctor or pharmacist before starting. Adaptogens are gentle, but "gentle" is not the same as "inert".
